To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neutrinos from the cooling PNSs are a new window to the physics of the supernovae, and that PINGU, Hyper-Kamiokade, and IceCube are sensitive to these neutrinos.

neutrino emission from the wind of a newly born PNS is a promising probe for the PNS magnetic field and rotation rate and that neutrino observations from nearby supernovae will enable us to probe the PNS magnetic acceleration and nucleosynthesis.
neutrinos with energy of order 1 GeV may be emitted from rotating protoneuron stars born during the gravitational collapse of massive stars.
In summary, our research is concerned with
neutrino emission from a new class of relativistic magnetized wind driven from rotating PNSs.
the detection of neutrinos from core collapse supernovae, and the study of the properties of the neutrino source.
the study of quasithermal neutrino emission from rotating and magnetized protostars, which is a new and interesting aspect of the physics of supernovae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neutrinos from PNS rotation would be detected by PINGU and/or Hyper-Kamiokade.

the detection of GeV neutrinos from core-collapse supernovas would provide important clues for the physics of magnetic field acceleration, nucleosyntheis, the relation between core-collapse supernovæ and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and the properties of the newly born neutron star.

the detection of GeV and/or TeV neutrinos would provide a unique probe of the physics of the neutrino-driven supernova mechanism, nucleosynthesis in the supernova explosion and the properties of the newly born neutron star, which is the most massive object in the Universe.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

neutrino observations from nearby core-collapse SN can be used to probe the physics of the PNS and its magnetosphere, and that this can be done in the GeV energy range, even if no cosmic ray is accelerated.
the PNSs born during core collapse may be sources of GeV neutrinos.
we have proposed a new mechanism to generate GeV neutrinos from core-collapse supernovas and have shown that these neutrinos could be observed by current and next-generation neutrino detectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neutrinos are the most promising probe of the physics of the early evolution of the supernovae and the properties of neutron stars.
PINGU, with a large effective volume and a high energy threshold, is the most sensitive detector for GeV neutrinos from supernovae.
the neutrino spectrum from PNSs is much more complex than previously thought.
